slides.text: Dayavati of Tamora stood before a British soldier's rifle and did not move. Her courage in the 1930 Jungle Satyagraha made Tamora a place of pilgrimage — and brought Gandhi there in 1933 specifically to honour her village.
slides.visualDescription: Title card: Dayavati — a young Gond woman — standing before a British soldier with rifle raised. Forest behind her. Her chest forward. Not moving. The image of the Tamora Satyagraha's defining moment. Ink-wash, deep greens, defiance and grace.

slides.text: Tamora village, Mahasamund tehsil, 1930. A forest watchman filed a false complaint against the tribals of Tamora for cutting forest wood. The government machinery moved to punish — and the community refused to accept the false charge.
slides.visualDescription: Tamora village in 1930 — a tribal settlement surrounded by Sal forest. A forest watchman filing a false complaint at the British office. The machinery of colonial injustice moving. The community of Tamora receiving the news and gathering to decide: what now.

slides.text: The Tamora Jungle Satyagraha began — seventeen days of organised non-violent resistance. Under the leadership of Narayan Singh and others, the tribals and farmers of Mahasamund tehsil held their ground against lathi charges, looting, and bayonets.
slides.visualDescription: The Tamora Satyagraha assembling — farmers and tribals gathering in disciplined lines. Narayan Singh leading. The organisation of resistance visible in their formation. Seventeen days ahead of them. The Satyagraha as a sustained campaign, not a single act.

slides.text: Police arrived with lathis and bayonets. Crops were looted. Cattle seized. Houses entered without permission. The full apparatus of colonial punishment deployed against a village that had simply refused a false charge.
slides.visualDescription: Police lathi charge on the Tamora Satyagrahis. Crops being looted — grain carried away. Cattle seized. Houses violated. The violence of the colonial response to non-violent resistance. The asymmetry of power made brutally visible.

slides.text: The Satyagrahis did not break. Not on day one. Not on day seventeen. Each day they stood. Each day they were beaten and refused to retaliate. The non-violence of Tamora was not the non-violence of weakness — it was the non-violence of iron will.
slides.visualDescription: Day after day of the Tamora Satyagraha — each day a new line forming, a new lathi charge, a new standing. The faces changing slightly with each day — bruised, tired — but the line not breaking. Seventeen days of the same discipline. Iron will made visible.

slides.text: Amar Singh of Khamharmuda — beaten by police, ordered to shout 'Long live the King.' He shouted: 'Mahatma Gandhi ki Jai.' Beaten more. His wife stepped forward. Beaten alongside him. Neither changed their words.
slides.visualDescription: Amar Singh under police blows — his mouth forming Gandhi's name. His wife stepping from the crowd to stand beside him. Both being beaten. Both still shouting. The lathi cannot change what is in the mouth if the heart is fixed. A couple's unity as resistance.

slides.text: Then came Dayavati. A young Gond woman. When the soldiers advanced with their rifles, she did not step back. She stood. Chest forward. Eyes open. The rifle pointed at her heart. The soldier hesitated. She did not.
slides.visualDescription: Dayavati standing before the rifle — her posture: completely open, completely unafraid. The soldier with the rifle aimed, hesitating. The forest behind her. Other Satyagrahis watching. The moment stretching. The soldier unsure what to do with a person who is not afraid.

slides.text: The soldier did not fire. Dayavati did not move. The standoff that could have ended in her death instead became the defining image of the Tamora Satyagraha. A young Gond woman had faced a British rifle with her bare chest — and the rifle had blinked.
slides.visualDescription: The resolution of the standoff — the soldier lowering the rifle slightly, then stepping back. Dayavati still standing. The other Satyagrahis releasing breath they had held. The image of Dayavati and the rifle: the picture that will reach Gandhi and bring him to Tamora.

slides.text: The story of Tamora reached Gandhi. He heard about Amar Singh, about Dayavati, about the seventeen days. When planning the 1933 Harijan tour, Gandhi made a specific request: he wanted to go to Tamora. He wanted to see the village that stood.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi at Sevagram Ashram, 1933, planning his Harijan tour itinerary. The name Tamora being pointed out on the map. Gandhi's decision: he must go there. The village that stood for seventeen days in 1930 has earned the Mahatma's personal visit.

slides.text: November 26, 1933. Gandhi visits Tamora. The village that had stood for seventeen days against the full force of colonial punishment received The Mahatma. He came to them. They had earned this.
slides.visualDescription: November 26, 1933. Gandhi's motor arriving in Tamora village. The village assembled — farmers, tribals, women, children. The same faces that stood before bayonets in 1930, now receiving Gandhi in 1933. Three years between the violence and this honour.

slides.text: Gandhi met Amar Singh and his wife — the couple who shouted his name while being beaten. He met Dayavati — the woman who stood before the rifle. He sat with the ordinary people of an extraordinary village.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi meeting Amar Singh and his wife in Tamora — taking their hands, looking at them with deep recognition. Then meeting Dayavati — looking at this young woman who stood before a rifle. Gandhi seeing in them what he had preached his whole life: truth in a human face.

slides.text: Gandhi listened as the Tamora people told him about the seventeen days — the lathi charges, the looting, the bayonets, Amar Singh's slogan, Dayavati's stand. He listened completely. He asked questions. He was a student of their courage.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi seated in Tamora's village square, listening to the accounts of the 1930 Satyagraha. The elders speaking. Gandhi's face showing the quality of his listening — not passive, but active, engaged, learning. The greatest leader of India studying ordinary people.

slides.text: Gandhi declared Tamora as Gandhigram — Gandhi's Village. The name stuck. The village of Tamora became Gandhigram Tamora — a renaming that acknowledged what the people of this place had demonstrated about the power of organised non-violence.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi making the declaration: Tamora is now Gandhigram. The people of Tamora hearing it. The name being written on a board at the village entrance. The renaming as recognition — the highest honour Gandhi could give a village that had practised his method better than most.

slides.text: But Gandhi's purpose in the second visit was not just to honour the fighters. It was to fight untouchability — the deeper, older, more pervasive injustice. In Tamora itself, Gandhi met the Harijan families of the village.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi in Tamora's Harijan quarter — meeting the families who lived at the edge of the village, whose children could not enter the temple, whose touch was considered pollution. Gandhi sitting with them, eating with them. The Satyagrahis' village also has its own injustice.

slides.text: The paradox of Tamora: a village that stood bravely against British injustice also maintained its own internal injustice of untouchability. Gandhi saw this without judgement but without silence. The same courage needed for both battles.
slides.visualDescription: The paradox made visible — the same Tamora Satyagrahis who stood before bayonets, walking past the Harijan quarter without entering it. Gandhi pointing to this gently. Courage in one direction, habit in another. The need for the same Satyagraha turned inward.

slides.text: In the 1930 Jungle Satyagraha, caste lines had blurred — tribal and non-tribal, upper caste and Harijan stood in the same line before the lathis. Gandhi pointed to this: 'You already know how to be one. You did it in 1930. Do it now.'
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi speaking to the Tamora assembly — pointing back to their own 1930 Satyagraha as proof. The same people who stood together before bayonets can stand together in equality. Their own history as Gandhi's argument. The mirror of their courage held up.

slides.text: Dayavati — the woman who stood before the rifle — became a symbol for both the anti-colonial struggle and the anti-untouchability struggle. Her courage did not belong to one battle. It belonged to anyone facing unjust power with nothing but truth.
slides.visualDescription: Dayavati in 1933 — three years after her stand before the rifle. Older, but the same quality in her eyes. Gandhi sitting beside her. A woman who has already proven she has the courage for any Satyagraha. Both battles in one face.

slides.text: The Satnam Ashram of Pt. Sundarlal Sharma — located between Raipur and Dhamtari — was a living experiment in anti-untouchability. Satnami people, considered untouchable, lived, worked, and prayed there as equals. Gandhi visited and was deeply moved.
slides.visualDescription: The Satnam Ashram — a peaceful, functioning community of equals. Satnami people and upper-caste people doing the same work, eating from the same kitchen, praying in the same space. Gandhi walking through it. What Pt. Sharma had built: proof of concept for Gandhi's mission.

slides.text: At the Satnam Ashram, Gandhi said: 'Harijan Uddhar mein aap mere bhi guru hain.' You are even my Guru in the salvation of Harijans. He said this to Pt. Sundarlal Sharma — the man who brought Gandhi to Chhattisgarh in the first place.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi at the Satnam Ashram, facing Pt. Sundarlal Sharma. The words spoken: Harijan Uddhar mein aap mere bhi guru hain. Sharma's face — moved, humble, complete. The student of Sharma acknowledging his teacher. The circle of the two visits closing.

slides.text: Sharma had been doing this work since before the Congress took it up. Since before Gandhi made it his central cause. For nearly two decades, Sharma had been placing the sacred thread on Harijan men, opening temples, building the Satnam Ashram.
slides.visualDescription: Pt. Sundarlal Sharma through two decades — the Janeu ceremony 1910s, the temple openings 1920s, the Satnam Ashram 1930s. A man who chose one cause and pursued it across twenty years without wavering. Gandhi's guru in the most literal sense.

slides.text: The Tamora visit and the Satnam Ashram visit in one day — both connected to the same truth. The tribals who stood before bayonets, the Satnami who prayed as equals, the Harijan children who ate beside the Mahatma: different faces of the same dignity.
slides.visualDescription: Three images in one frame: Dayavati before the rifle, the Satnam Ashram community at prayer, Harijan children eating with Gandhi. Three faces of the same truth. The dignity that Satyagraha demands: inward as well as outward. The full mission visible.

slides.text: The village circuits of November 26-27 took Gandhi through Tamora, Devri, Kurud — village after village where untouchability was practised and where Gandhi gently, firmly, pointed to the contradiction between freedom from the British and bondage to caste.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi's motor moving through the village circuits — Tamora, Devri, Kurud. At each village, the same meeting with Harijan families, the same gentle pointing to the contradiction. The motor as a vehicle of conscience moving through the Chhattisgarh countryside.

slides.text: At Devri, a village entirely of Chamars — the leather-working community considered untouchable — Gandhi ate with the community and spoke for two hours. The village had never received a visitor of Gandhi's stature. He treated it as the most important stop.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi in Devri village — a community of Chamars receiving him. Gandhi sitting on the ground with them, eating together, speaking for two hours. Treating this village of the 'lowest' caste as the most important destination on his itinerary. Radical equality in practice.

slides.text: At Kurud, the caste Hindus opened the temple doors to Harijans in Gandhi's presence. A door that had been closed for centuries, opened in one afternoon. Gandhi did not open it himself — he stood witness as the community chose to open it.
slides.visualDescription: The Kurud temple — ancient doors that have been closed to Harijans for centuries. The caste Hindu community in Gandhi's presence deciding to open them. The doors opening slowly. Harijan families entering for the first time. Gandhi watching as a witness, not an actor.

slides.text: The temple door as a metaphor and as a literal act. The Harijans who entered Kurud temple on November 27, 1933, were the first of their community to do so. What they experienced in that moment — the right to stand before the same God — cannot be calculated.
slides.visualDescription: Harijan families entering the Kurud temple — their feet on the threshold, the interior visible for the first time. Their faces: the particular expression of a person crossing a boundary that was placed there before their birth. The door as the boundary of dignity.

slides.text: Gandhi collected funds for the Harijan Sevak Sangh throughout the village circuits. Not just witness and words — practical support for the ongoing work of uplift. The Tilak Fund of 1920 replaced by the Harijan Fund of 1933. Different cause, same method.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi collecting for the Harijan Sevak Sangh in the village circuit — people donating. The Harijan Fund bag filling as the Tilak Fund bag had filled thirteen years before. The method unchanged. The cause deepened. Same hands giving for a deeper freedom.

slides.text: Dayavati's village received Gandhi. Amar Singh's village received Gandhi. Sharma's Satnam Ashram received Gandhi. Each place had proven something about the possibility of human dignity — and Gandhi came to each to confirm what they already knew.
slides.visualDescription: The three sites of the day: Tamora, the Satnam Ashram, Kurud. Each a proof of concept. Each a place where something true had already happened. Gandhi arriving at each not to create but to confirm. The Mahatma as witness to what the people had already built.

slides.text: What the fire of Tamora proved in 1930: that organised non-violence in the face of armed colonial power works. What Gandhi proved in 1933: that the same organised non-violence, turned inward against caste, works too. One fire, two battles.
slides.visualDescription: The fire of Tamora — 1930 and 1933 in one visual. The external fire of anti-colonial resistance. The internal fire of anti-caste work. One flame. Two directions. Dayavati standing before the rifle in 1930. The temple doors opening in 1933. The same fire.

slides.text: Narayan Singh, who led the Tamora Satyagraha, sat with Gandhi in 1933 and described the seventeen days. Gandhi listened and said: 'You have done more than most people who call themselves Satyagrahis.' The student honouring the practitioners.
slides.visualDescription: Narayan Singh and Gandhi in conversation in Tamora, 1933. Narayan Singh describing the seventeen days. Gandhi listening with the intensity that distinguishes his listening. Then Gandhi's words of honour. The practitioners being seen by the theorist who created the method.

slides.text: The Tamora Jungle Satyagraha of 1930 is not in any national history book. Dayavati's name is not in any national hall of fame. Amar Singh's slogan is not quoted by any national politician. But in Gandhigram Tamora — the village still knows.
slides.visualDescription: Present-day Gandhigram Tamora — a village with its renamed identity. The elders who remember, or whose parents remembered. The story passed down in households. No national recognition. Only the village's own knowledge of what it did and what it proved.

slides.text: Gandhi named it Gandhigram as a gift. But the true gift was given the other way: Tamora gave Gandhi the living proof that his method worked when practised by ordinary people in extreme circumstances, without his presence, without his guidance.
slides.visualDescription: The naming ceremony in reverse — Tamora giving Gandhi the proof he needed. The gift flowing from the village to the man, not only from the man to the village. The Satyagraha that worked without Gandhi proving that the idea had taken root independently.

slides.text: The 1930 Jungle Satyagrahas across Chhattisgarh — Tamora, Nagari-Sihawa, others — demonstrated that the Gandhian method had become genuinely the people's own. No longer dependent on the Mahatma's physical presence. The tool had been inherited.
slides.visualDescription: A map of Chhattisgarh showing all the 1930 Jungle Satyagraha sites — Tamora, Nagari-Sihawa, others. Each site a proof. The method distributed across the land. Gandhi's physical absence between 1920 and 1933 irrelevant — the idea had been planted and grown.

slides.text: Dayavati. A Gond woman who stood before a British rifle in 1930. A woman whose village was named for Gandhi by Gandhi himself in 1933. A woman whose name is known only in her own district. The measure of Chhattisgarh's unrecognised heroism.
slides.visualDescription: Portrait of Dayavati — a woman the nation does not know. Her face carrying what she did: the quality of someone who has stood before the worst and not moved. Her village renamed Gandhigram behind her. The unrecognised heroine as the face of an unrecognised movement.

slides.text: The forest of Tamora still stands. The Sal trees that the watchman falsely claimed were cut still grow. The village that refused to accept a false charge is still there — older, poorer in some ways, richer in the one way that matters.
slides.visualDescription: Present-day Tamora — Sal forest around the village. The trees that were the subject of the 1930 false charge, still standing. The village, still there. Still with its story, still with its knowledge of what happened here, still Gandhigram.

slides.text: In these five days of the second visit, Gandhi also made a promise to Chhattisgarh. He promised to return to Bilaspur. He never did. But the promise was made in good faith, and the people of Bilaspur kept faith with it regardless.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhi making his promise to return to Bilaspur — the leaders of Bilaspur receiving it with gratitude. The promise that history will not allow to be kept. Gandhi's death in 1948 ending all return journeys. But the faith kept by Bilaspur regardless.

slides.text: The fire of Tamora — lit in 1930 — burned for decades. Every freedom fighter in Chhattisgarh who came after knew the story. It was the proof that the method worked. It was the flame that did not need Gandhi to keep burning.
slides.visualDescription: The fire metaphor made literal and beautiful — a flame in the Tamora forest, burning independently. Around it: the faces of the 1930 Satyagrahis, and then the faces of those who came after, inspired by the story. The flame passed from hand to hand.

slides.text: Tamora: renamed Gandhigram. Dayavati: undefeated. The fire: still burning. Next: Episode 3 — The Mahatma at the Door.
slides.visualDescription: Gandhigram Tamora at dusk — the renamed village, the unchanged forest, the permanent fire. Title card appearing: Episode 3 — The Mahatma at the Door. The temple doors of Chhattisgarh about to open.
